# Genuine hinge contact transfers cap mass through a density repair

This note gives an exact bridge from stop-loss inequalities to cap
probabilities. It requires equality at the actual threshold, and does
not infer that equality from the existing physical surface stress.

## 1. Contact of two stop-loss curves

Let `alpha,beta` be finite equal-mass measures on a compact subset of
Euclidean space, with `alpha<=cx beta`. Fix an affine functional `ell`
and define

```
C_alpha(t)=integral (ell(w)-t)_+ d alpha(w),
C_beta(t)=integral (ell(w)-t)_+ d beta(w).
```

Then `D(t)=C_beta(t)-C_alpha(t)>=0` for every real `t`. Suppose
`D(t0)=0`. The one-sided derivatives of the individual curves are

```
C_alpha'(t0-) = -alpha{ell>=t0},
C_alpha'(t0+) = -alpha{ell>t0},
```

and similarly for `beta`. These follow by bounded convergence of the
one-sided difference quotients; their absolute values are bounded by
the total mass. Since `D` attains its minimum zero at `t0`,
`D'(t0-)<=0<=D'(t0+)`. Consequently

```
beta{ell>=t0} >= alpha{ell>=t0},
beta{ell>t0} <= alpha{ell>t0}.                            (1)
```

In particular, if `beta{ell=t0}=0`, then both inequalities force

```
alpha{ell=t0}=0,
beta{ell>=t0}=alpha{ell>=t0},
beta{ell>t0}=alpha{ell>t0}.                              (2)
```

Thus genuine stop-loss contact and a boundary-null repaired measure
give exact cap transfer. Without contact, differentiating the
inequality `D>=0` is invalid. Without boundary-nullness, only the two
different inequalities (1) follow.

For any martingale realizing `alpha<=cx beta`, equality of this
hinge integral also gives a rowwise noncrossing statement by equality
in conditional Jensen. If a source has `ell<t0`, its destinations
have `ell<=t0`; if it has `ell>t0`, destinations have `ell>=t0`;
if it has `ell=t0`, all destinations have `ell=t0`. Sources on one
strict side may still send mass to the plane, explaining why the
closed and open inequalities differ in (1).

## 2. An actual auxiliary optimization supplies the required contact

Let `P` be a compact fixed-marginal endpoint coupling class, possibly
with closed support-roof or other proved Jensen-contact constraints.
Let `rho_pi` denote its midpoint law. Fix finitely many affine
functionals `ell_j`, thresholds `t_j`, and positive weights `c_j`.
Choose an actual maximizer `pi0` of

```
integral Phi d rho_pi,
Phi(w)=sum_j c_j(ell_j(w)-t_j)_+.
```

Existence follows from compactness and continuity of this bounded
cost on the compact midpoint range. Suppose a density-repair theorem
provides `pi1 in P` with `rho_pi0<=cx rho_pi1`. Maximality and convex
order give equality of the two `Phi` integrals. Every individual
hinge-integral difference is nonnegative, and every `c_j` is positive,
so each difference is zero separately.

The conclusions (1) hold for every selected threshold. If the repaired
law gives no mass to the selected hyperplanes, (2) holds for all of
them. Thus every selected cap mass is preserved exactly.

This observation applies to the contact-constrained weighted repair
as well as to the unweighted one. It also applies to a repair with
a quantitative overcapacity budget: exact domination by the baseline
capacity is not required for the contact argument. A fixed coarse
domination by a boundary-null reference suffices to deduce (2).

The maximization here is a genuine additional transport problem. It
does not say that an arbitrary coupling from the selected body stress
already maximizes these hinges. Such a claim would require a separate
variational argument retaining the actual endpoint and source budgets.

### 2.1. The hinge maximizer can retain an actual marked source budget

Let `nu` be a fixed finite source law of the same mass as every midpoint
law in `P`, and assume a source-compatible old coupling exists. Define

```
P_nu={pi in P: nu<=cx rho_pi}.
```

This class is compact: each convex-order test is a weakly closed
inequality against a continuous function on the common compact range,
and `P` is compact. It is nonempty by assumption. Consequently the
positive weighted hinge objective has an attained maximum `pi0` over
`P_nu`.

Suppose the arbitrary-old-law repair theorem applies to every coupling
in `P`. Apply it to this `pi0`, obtaining `pi1 in P` with
`rho_pi0<=cx rho_pi1`. Transitivity gives
`nu<=cx rho_pi1`, so `pi1` remains in `P_nu`. Therefore maximality
over `P_nu` gives all the hinge contacts and cap-transfer statements
from Section 2 without any change.

There are two different optimizations in this argument. The auxiliary
hinge maximum may include the constraint `nu<=cx rho`. The internal
strongly convex surplus optimizations used to prove the arbitrary-old
repair theorem need not, and must not silently be assumed to, include
that constraint. The repair theorem is applied after the hinge
maximizer has been chosen; its final convex-order improvement preserves
source compatibility by transitivity. Thus no invalid local variation
of a source-constrained optimizer is used.

If a source mark has a prescribed physical conditional barycenter,
represent its law by `nu` and choose the corresponding martingale to
`rho_pi0`. Lifting through the fixed conditional mark law retains the
mark distribution and that conditional barycenter. Composing with a
martingale from `rho_pi0` to `rho_pi1` preserves them again. One may
then draw the new endpoint pair conditional on its midpoint to realize
`pi1`. Additional normal and parity labels are retained by applying
this construction separately in those conditional classes. This does
not promise to retain a different pre-existing mark-to-midpoint joint
law when replacing it by the newly chosen hinge-maximizing law.

Thus a PRE-EXISTING cap-paying coupling that also genuinely maximizes
the selected positive weighted hinge objective in the source-compatible
class admits a faithful density repair for those selected caps, under
the boundary-null assumption of (2). Maximization by itself supplies
no proof that its chosen old law has the required cap payment.

### 2.2. Arbitrary old cap payment cannot be retained in general

The last qualification is necessary, even with no old boundary mass.
Take the actual mixed convex body

```
C=[-1,1] x [-1,1] subset R x R,
```

with endpoint marginals given by length measure on the integer fibers
at bases `-1` and `1`. Each has mass two and density one. The
antithetic coupling sends continuous coordinates `x` and `-x` to one
another, so its midpoint law is

```
rho_pre=2 delta_(0,0).
```

Use this as the physical source law `nu`; the old marked martingale
may simply be the identity. Every possible coupling of the endpoint
marginals has midpoint base zero and midpoint continuous coordinate
in `[-1,1]`. If a repaired midpoint law is dominated by length measure
on that interval and has mass two, it must be exactly that full
length measure. It dominates `nu` in convex order, since its mean is
zero.

For the closed ambient halfspace `H={x>=-1/2}`,

```
rho_pre(H)=2,
rho_repaired(H)=3/2.
```

Neither law has mass on the boundary `x=-1/2`. Thus no general rule can
preserve arbitrary old cap payment while imposing the sharp density
ceiling, even though the source, all endpoint marginals, integer
midpoint membership, and actual target fiber are retained. The loss
cannot be blamed solely on a point source lying on the cap boundary.

This example does not contradict the hinge-maximizer result: for this
threshold the antithetic coupling does not maximize the positive hinge
integral. Nor is it an OC counterexample.

## 3. Exact threshold derivatives for a capped transport value

Let `D` be a compact family of feasible midpoint laws on a compact
physical set, and assume every law is dominated by `B omega` for one
fixed finite measure `omega` and finite constant `B`. Let

```
V(t)=max_(rho in D) sum_j c_j integral(ell_j-t_j)_+ d rho,
```

where `t=(t_1,...,t_N)`. Suppose

```
omega{ell_j=t_j}=0  for every j.                           (3)
```

Let `A(t)` be the compact set of maximizing laws at `t`. For every
direction `v in R^N`, the one-sided directional derivative exists
and is

```
V'(t;v)
 = max_(rho in A(t)) [-sum_j c_j v_j rho{ell_j>=t_j}].       (4)
```

Here is the uniformity needed for this formula. The error after
subtracting the linear expansion of one hinge at threshold `t_j`
has absolute value at most

```
|epsilon v_j| 1_{|ell_j-t_j|<=|epsilon v_j|}.
```

Its integral against any `rho in D` is therefore at most `B` times
the same integral against `omega`, which is `o(|epsilon|)` uniformly
by (3). The threshold derivative of the objective is consequently
uniform over `D`.

The lower bound in (4) follows by retaining any fixed maximizing law
at `t`. For the upper bound take maximizers at `t+epsilon v` and
extract a weakly convergent subsequence. Continuity of the hinge
cost shows that the limit is in `A(t)`. The cap integrals also
converge: the limiting law is dominated by `B omega`, so its mass
on each boundary in (3) is zero, and bounded halfspace indicators
are continuity tests for this weak convergence. Combining this
with the uniform expansion proves the upper bound in (4).

If the density-repair theorem implies that unrestricted and capped
transport maxima agree for every convex cost, this is also the
directional derivative of the unrestricted optimal value. The
formula retains a maximum over all maximizing laws, unless uniqueness
or equality of their cap vectors has been separately proved.

## 4. Boundary mass can be retained by shifted hinges on the actual graph

There is a useful stronger version for the normal-preserving surface
repairs in this workspace. Let `P` be the finite set of actual integer
bases, let `K_z` be positive full-dimensional fibers in `R^d`, and let
`eta` be their actual surface measure with the normal label retained.
At a fixed normal `n`, every admissible midpoint is assumed to lie on
the actual graph

```
G_n = union_(z in P) ({z} x K_z(n)),
```

where `K_z(n)` is the exposed face with normal `n`. Suppose the
repaired laws are dominated by a finite multiple of a weighted
reference measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to
`eta`. The exact surface repairs and the discounted repair with its
coarse bound have this property.

Fix an ambient cap functional

```
ell(z,x)=a dot z+v dot x-b.
```

We can choose finitely many hinge thresholds at almost every normal
so that genuine contact for those hinges preserves BOTH the original
closed-cap and open-cap mass, including any mass on `ell=0`.

### 4.1. Nonzero continuous normal

Assume `v!=0`. Apart from the two normals `n=+v/|v|` and
`n=-v/|v|`, the cut plane has zero `eta` mass. Here is the needed
measure justification. For one convex body's rectifiable boundary,
a measurable positive-surface-measure subset lying in a fixed
hyperplane has the same approximate tangent plane as that hyperplane
at almost every density point of the subset. At surface-regular
points this is the body's tangent plane. Its outward normal must
therefore be one of the two normals to the hyperplane. Singular
boundary points have surface measure zero. Summing the finitely many
fibers proves the assertion. Disintegration then gives zero
conditional plane mass at almost every OTHER normal. We do not claim
this for every individual lower-dimensional conditional face.

At those ordinary normals, use the original threshold zero and the
single hinge `ell_+`. The contact lemma transfers both cap masses,
since the repaired reference gives no mass to the plane.

At either exceptional parallel normal, the value of `ell` is constant
on each exposed face. More explicitly its finite possible values are

```
q_z(n)=a dot z + |v| h_(K_z)(n)-b      if n=+v/|v|,
q_z(n)=a dot z - |v| h_(K_z)(n)-b      if n=-v/|v|.
```

Choose `delta>0` strictly below all nonzero `|q_z(n)|`; if all are
zero choose any positive `delta`. On the ENTIRE actual output graph,

```
{ell>=0}={ell>=-delta},
{ell>0} ={ell>= delta}.                                  (5)
```

Neither shifted plane `ell=-delta` nor `ell=delta` meets `G_n`.
Include BOTH hinges `(ell+delta)_+` and `(ell-delta)_+`, each with
a positive weight, in the objective. Genuine contact for them gives
exact transfer of the two shifted cap masses and hence, by (5), of
the original closed and open cap masses. Their difference transfers
the mass on the original plane as well. This includes normal atoms
carrying whole facets; no boundary-null assumption at threshold zero
is made.

### 4.2. Pure base caps

If `v=0`, the values `q_z=a dot z-b` are finite in number at EVERY
normal. The same two-threshold construction works with one `delta`
chosen from that finite set, independently of the normal. Thus pure
base caps, including those carrying whole fibers on their boundary,
are covered too.

### 4.3. Finite menus, actual inward selectors, and exact quantifiers

For a finite cap menu, combine all the one- or two-hinge choices just
described with strictly positive coefficients. The threshold choices
are Borel in the normal: for a cap with `v!=0` they use zero away
from two fixed normal points and fixed finite-gap values at those
points; pure base caps use fixed thresholds. At each normal and
original parity class choose an attained maximizer of this objective
over the compact source-compatible class from Section 2.1. Its
arbitrary-old-law density repair remains in that class, so every
included hinge has contact. The preceding argument then transfers
every selected open and closed cap mass exactly, conditional on that
normal and parity class. Integration preserves the global masses.

The objective is continuous in the compact physical coupling
variables and Borel in the normal parameter. The already established
compact-kernel measurable maximization/selection construction applies
to these conditional classes; equivalently include the attained
optimal-value equality as one more Borel compact constraint. The
argument does not require a measurable face frame or a division by a
conditional surface density.

More explicitly, write the conditional feasible classes in one fixed
compact coupling space by countably many inequalities
`c_j(n,pi)<=0`, continuous in `pi` and Borel in `n`. Fix a countable
dense subset of that space. For each integer `k`, take the supremum
of the continuous objective over dense points satisfying
`c_j(n,pi)<1/k` for `j<=k`. This is a Borel countable supremum.
The strict relaxed sets are open and contain every exactly feasible
point, so the dense-point supremum equals their full supremum.
Compactness shows that their decreasing limit is exactly the maximum
over the true feasible class. Its value is therefore Borel. Adding
the equality to that value gives a nonempty compact class to which
the established selector applies.

In particular it preserves the ACTUAL inward-erosion cap selector.
Away from the cut plane that selector is the usual cap indicator.
On a coincident outside support face, `n=+v/|v|`, inward erosion
contributes zero and the selector is the open-cap indicator. On a
coincident inside support face, `n=-v/|v|`, inward erosion removes
inside-cap mass and the selector is the closed-cap indicator. Both
are among the quantities just preserved. Pure base cap selectors
that use the fixed closed or fixed open convention are also covered.

This does NOT preserve an arbitrary measurable facet allocation
`theta(n,z,x)` with values between zero and one: open and closed
mass alone do not determine its integral. The statement is for the
actual inward selector, or for another selector that is known to be
one of those two conventions at the corresponding normal.

Finally, the chosen law must genuinely be a maximizer of this
normal-dependent positive hinge objective in the source-compatible
class. None of this proves that an arbitrary pre-existing cap-paying
law is such a maximizer or that the maximizer has the cap payment
needed for OC. The exact obstruction in Section 2.2 remains relevant.

## 5. Scope for a selected-minimum proof

These statements identify an exact mechanism that can legitimately
turn a transport stop-loss inequality into a cap comparison. Its
required inputs are an attained hinge optimization or another proved
hinge-contact equality, and correct handling of boundary mass.

The existing normal-convex surface stress by itself gives inequalities
against hinges. It does not supply their equality at the desired
critical thresholds. Nor does (4) identify a deterministic point of
the mixed-integer set. Those obligations remain outside this note.
